title: The Ones That Live in You

t: You are carrying about as many bacterial cells as human ones. Right now.
The number of bacterial cells you carry is roughly comparable to the number of your own — and they are not passengers you would be better off without.
sub: And you would be very ill without them.
That last part is the surprising half, and it took a long time to establish.

question: What would happen to an animal raised with no bacteria at all?
How does a germ-free animal differ from a normal one?
options: It would develop abnormally and be unhealthy
It would be perfectly healthy and never get ill
stages.outcome: It would develop abnormally and be unhealthy
note: Guess before you look. The intuitive answer is the second one.
Commit. Germ-free animals can be raised, which makes this an experiment rather than a thought experiment.

t: Match each thing your bacteria do to why it matters.
Each of these is a service performed by resident microbes rather than by you.

label: You cannot digest it yourself
Releases energy from plant material no human enzyme can break
You cannot make these either
Supplies vitamin K and several B vitamins
Leaves no room for anything worse
Competitive exclusion of pathogens

t: The bacteria living on and in you are called your microbiome.
The community of microbes you carry is your microbiome, and it is best thought of as an organ you were not born with.
The microbiome is acquired after birth, differs between individuals, and performs metabolic and immunological functions the host genome does not encode.

It is inherited horizontally rather than vertically — from birth canal, milk, food and environment rather than from your genome — which makes it unlike any other part of you and means it can be lost, damaged and in principle restored.
sub: Germ-free animals grow up with immune systems that do not work properly.
Animals raised sterile develop abnormal gut structure, poor immune calibration and altered behaviour — the community is doing developmental work, not just living there.
Which is why the hygiene hypothesis is taken seriously: too little early exposure appears to leave immune tolerance badly set.

The evidence is suggestive rather than settled, and the popular version overstates it considerably. What is well established is that germ-free animals are abnormal; what is still contested is how much of the rise in allergy and autoimmunity in wealthy countries that explains.

q: Are the bacteria living in you a bad thing?
Is the resident microbiota harmful, harmless or necessary?
In what sense is the microbiome functionally part of the organism?
options: No — you need them, and you are unhealthy without them
They make no difference either way
why: They do jobs you cannot do yourself: getting energy out of food you cannot digest, making vitamins you cannot make, and teaching your defences what to leave alone.

They are necessary. Germ-free animals are demonstrably abnormal — poorly developed guts, miscalibrated immune systems — which establishes that the community is doing work the host depends on rather than merely tolerating it.

It supplies metabolic capability absent from the host genome and participates in host development, which is a functional rather than a rhetorical sense of 'part of'. It is also why broad-spectrum antibiotics have consequences beyond the infection they treat: they are not selective about which community members they remove.

t: One of the most effective treatments for a serious gut infection is a transplant of someone else's gut bacteria.

Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, which follows antibiotics wiping out the resident community, is cured in around 90% of cases by faecal microbiota transplant — better than any antibiotic. It works by restoring the community that was competitively excluding the pathogen, which is about as direct a demonstration as one could want that the microbiome is doing a job.
